title: Spanish Ladies
description: The sailors' farewell to Spain, for 2 to 4 singers, as Cecil Sharp took it down from Captain Lewis of Minehead and printed it in 1909. Everyone sings verse 1 and then the chorus, "We will rant and we'll roar", twice, on Sharp's own harmony, with the soprano carrying the tune. A capstan shanty in the old minor mode; the last chord turns major, as Sharp's piano postlude does.

credits.words: traditional sea shanty (as sung by Captain Lewis, Minehead; printed 1909)
credits.tune: traditional sea shanty (as sung by Captain Lewis, Minehead; printed 1909)

licence.words: public domain: traditional, verse 1 and the chorus as Cecil J. Sharp printed them in 1909 from the singing of Captain Lewis of Minehead (Folk Songs from Somerset, Fifth Series, No. CXXIV); every line is in print before 1909, with small differences: verse 1 and chorus lines 3 and 4 in Robert Bell, Ancient Poems, Ballads and Songs of the Peasantry of England (London: John W. Parker and Son, 1857), p. 234, and in Christopher Stone, Sea Songs and Ballads (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1906), No. 91; chorus line 1 ("We'll rant and we'll roar, like true British sailors") in Frederick Marryat, Poor Jack (London: Longman, 1840), p. 116; and "all on the salt seas" and chorus line 4 in W. Chappell, Popular Music of the Olden Time, vol. 2 (London: Cramer, Beale & Chappell, 1859), p. 737; so none of them is Lieut. Kettlewell's alone (Sharp's note, p. 90: Kettlewell "revised Captain Lewis's words"); Sharp's verses 2 to 5 are left out
licence.tune: public domain: traditional, printed 1909 by Cecil J. Sharp (died 1924)
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella on the harmony of Sharp's piano accompaniment (public domain: Sharp died 1924): the soprano is his voice part note for note; the alto, tenor and bass sing one note a syllable on the chords of his accompaniment, his left hand for the bass; at printed pitch; breaths written in for beginners; the last sung chord is A major, the chord of Sharp's piano postlude (under the voice he has A minor), an arranger's choice
licence.source: tune, words and harmony from Cecil J. Sharp, Folk Songs from Somerset, Fifth Series (London: Simpkin & Co.; Schott & Co.; Taunton: Barnicott and Pearce, 1909), No. CXXIV, "Spanish Ladies. Sea Chanty", pp. 62 to 64, the voice part and Sharp's piano accompaniment, with his note on pp. 89 and 90 ("Words and air from Captain Lewis, of Minehead"; a capstan chanty, which Captain Lewis sang "as a song" at about crotchet = 112); printed with no key signature (A aeolian), 3/4, Moderato, and written here at the printed pitch, in A minor; verse 1 and the chorus; read from the scan at archive.org/details/imslp-songs-from-somerset-sharp-cecil. Verse 1 and the chorus checked against W. B. Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (3rd ed., Glasgow: James Brown & Son, 1913), "Farewell and Adieu", p. 26, archive.org/details/shipsseasongssha00whal
